"Noor, listen to this." Hafsa tapped her psychology textbook on the kitchen table.
"Can I eat first, Hafsa Appi?"
"Old experiment. People were told they were helping test memory. Every time a stranger in the next room got an answer wrong, they pressed a switch that gave him an electric shock. Bigger each time."
"Real shocks?"
"No, he was an actor, but they didn't know that. He shouted, he banged on the wall. And a man in a grey coat just said, 'Please continue.'"
"And they stopped, obviously."
"Most didn't. Most went all the way."
Noor put her spoon down. "They must have been horrible people."
"That's what I thought. But the book says they were ordinary. Teachers, clerks. Sweating, arguing, laughing nervously, and still pressing."
"You'd never."
Hafsa was quiet. "I don't know, Noor. I do whatever the class rep says without asking. I think that's the scary part."

qa.a: Hafsa feels uneasy, realising the people who kept pressing were ordinary, and since she does whatever the class rep says without asking, she might comply too.

Class note, third-year sociology, Tuesday. Urmila Rao.
We covered the classic obedience studies today: the switches, the actor's cries, the researcher's calm phrases. Most students reacted as usual, shocked at 'those people'. Darshan did not. He sat very still, then put his hand up: 'Ma'am, none of them sounded like villains. They kept asking "Is he all right?" and then carried on.' A few laughed. He didn't. Later he added, 'My uncle works in a shop. The owner tells him to short-weigh customers, and he does it, and he's the kindest person I know.' He looked angry, more with himself than anyone.
What I did next: I stayed back with him for ten minutes, then set the class a short writing task for Thursday: describe one small order you followed that you now doubt. I'll read them privately.

passage: I'm Yamini. In my final year I was head marshal for our college's cultural fest, with a neon vest, a lanyard and a walkie-talkie. No teacher checked on us after the first briefing. It was the vest, the walkie-talkie, the fact that nobody asked what we were doing. Months later Vaibhav told me he nearly quit the fest club because of me. I apologised. I'm still working out how easily I became that person.

passage:
Warden's note, 22 Sept. Vasudha Menon.
Parul (20, second year) was made mess monitor in July. Early on she was fair and even joked with the first-years. Over the past weeks I have watched her change. She now stands at the mess door with the monitor's register and turns back juniors who arrive two minutes late, even when food is left. Tonight she made a first-year, Rinku, wait outside while the others ate, and when I asked why, she said, 'They take advantage otherwise, ma'am. They need to learn.' She believed it. The juniors now go silent when she passes.
What I did next: I spoke with Parul privately and asked how she would have felt last year. I changed the rule so monitors report lateness to me instead of turning anyone away, and I'll rotate the role monthly.

qa.a: Vasudha had monitors report lateness instead of turning anyone away and will rotate the role monthly, adding a check and limiting how long one person holds the power.

qa.a: The juniors seem wary of Parul, going silent whenever she passes.

passage: Honestly, Rafiq, the strangest part of the hotel traineeship wasn't the hours. It was the name. For six months I was 'trainee'. 'Trainee, towels.' 'Trainee, don't speak to guests unless asked.' We wore grey while staff wore blue. At first I kept a notebook of ideas, like moving the breakfast queue so it didn't block the lift. By month three I'd stopped writing in it. By month five, when a guest asked me something simple about check-out, I heard myself say, 'Sorry, I'm only the trainee, ask the desk.' I knew the answer. I'd just started believing I wasn't the kind of person who answers. And underneath, I was angry all the time at everyone in blue. The first time anyone there called me Jahnavi was my last day.

qa.a: Trainees wore grey while staff wore blue.

qa.a: Jahnavi had come to feel small in the role, believing trainees are not the kind of people who answer.

qa.a: Jahnavi could pick up the notebook of ideas again, since it was the habit that kept Jahnavi's own voice alive before the role took over.

I've roomed with Nandini since the first week of engineering college, so I watched it happen, though I can't say what was in her head. In August she arrived with a guitar and a hundred plans. Then came 'fresher period': seniors decided where first-years sat in the mess, what they wore on Mondays, when they could use the common room. Nandini followed all of it. By October she'd stopped taking the guitar out. When the class rep asked for fest volunteers, she said, 'Freshers don't get picked anyway.' Once, a senior she'd never met asked her to fetch his bag, and she just went, without a word, face flat. At night she started saying 'we're just juniors' about things that had nothing to do with seniors. I don't know exactly when she started believing it.
— Sunaina

Day 1. Irfan, twenty-one, walked into the bank branch in a new shirt, carrying a list of questions. "Can I sit in on the loan desk?" The branch head laughed. "Trainees do photocopies." Pooja, the other trainee, rolled her eyes at him, friendly. "Welcome."
Week 4. The list of questions was gone. People called Irfan 'photocopy boy'. When a customer asked him about an account form, he pointed at the counter without looking up. At lunch Pooja said, "You used to talk more." He shrugged. "What's the point? We're furniture."
Week 8. Irfan snapped at the peon over a jammed machine, then sat staring at the queue, jaw tight. That night he wrote in his notebook: 'Maybe I'm just not a bank person.' He had forgotten the list of questions entirely.

passage: I'm Sarita. Last spring my college friend Kartik became a shift supervisor at the call centre where I also work. Kartik is the person who remembers everyone's birthday and cries at weddings.
